newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy on the warpath over EMU forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Italy on the warpath over EMU forecasts.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi slammed the European Commission on Wednesday for forecasting that Italy would fall short of tough criteria laid down for founder members of economic and monetary union (EMU).
Coalition allies joined the attack, accusing the European Union executive of playing politics and not sticking to financial fundamentals.
But centre-right opposition parties said the Brussels forecasts had exposed the government's incompetence.

The Commission incurred Prodi's wrath by predicting that the ratio between Italy's budget deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) would hit 3.2 percent this year and 3.9 percent in 1998, compared with the three percent target laid down by the Maastricht Treaty.
The only other EU country set to miss the deficit target was Greece, the Commission said.

However, it did add: "This (3.2 percent for Italy) may become 3.0 percent of GDP if the (budgetary) measures already taken have full effectiveness and, if necessary, additional measures are introduced."

In a statement, Prodi commented: "The Commission's decision to forecast at this stage a financial unbalance, albeit minimal, in a member state that has already taken necessary and correct steps to cut the deficit...is incomprehensible."
Prodi, who has promised to resign if Italy fails to make the EMU grade, said the forecast did not take into account all the available budget data.

"The government...is deeply committed to following its own action of structural reform which will enable Italy to arrive at the single currency date with all its papers in order," said the statement, released as Prodi left on an official trip to Kuwait.
A decision is due to be made in May 1998 on which European Union states should qualify for monetary union on the basis of their 1997 economic performance.

Italy, burdened by a huge debt mountain, had a deficit/GDP ratio of 6.7 percent in 1996 and the government has introduced deficit-cutting measures worth some 78 trillion lire ($45.8 billion) over the past four months to meet the EMU target.
But the hard-right National Alliance said the Commission had showed Prodi's centre-left coalition was on the wrong track.
"Italy will only enter Europe if it changes its economic policy, which means changing the government majority," National Alliance leader Gianfranco Fini told reporters.
The hard-left Communist Refoundation, which secures Prodi's parliamentary majority, said the Commission had ignored Italy's true economic performance.
"These are purely political figures," said Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti, adding that the Commission was seeking to force the government into a radical overhaul of the welfare state.
Many budget measures introduced by Prodi's 11-month-old government are of a short-term nature.
International economic organisations have urged Italy to embark on a structural reform of social spending to guarantee stable accounts in future.
Talks between the government and unions on a reform of the welfare state should start before mid-May, union leaders said on Wednesday.
Communist Refoundation has warned that it will not accept any cuts in social spending.
"(The Commission) is exerting the most violent pressure on Italy to make it go down the wrong road and cut the welfare state," Bertinotti said.
